zea-plant.name: Teosinte
zea-plant.summary: The wild grass species native to Mesoamerica from which maize (Zea mays) was domesticated, belonging to the same genus, Zea.

mokaya.name: Mokaya
mokaya.summary: A pre-Olmec culture of Mexico's Soconusco region and the Pacific coast of Guatemala, among the earliest known settled societies in Mesoamerica.

three-sisters-agriculture.name: Three Sisters
three-sisters-agriculture.summary: A companion-planting method combining maize, beans and squash, in which each crop supports the others, developed by Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

zohapilco.name: Zohapilco
zohapilco.summary: An archaeological site in central Mexico dating from 5500 to 2200 BC, known for the earliest ceramics found there and links to the Tlatilco and Olmec cultures.

olmecs.name: Olmecs
olmecs.summary: An early Mesoamerican civilization that flourished roughly 1200 to 400 BC in what is now Veracruz and Tabasco, known for colossal stone heads and considered one of the cradles of civilization.

el-manat.name: El Manatí
el-manat.summary: An archaeological site in Veracruz, Mexico, a sacred Olmec sacrificial bog used from about 1600 to 1200 BCE, holding the oldest known wooden artifacts and rubber balls found in Mexico.

tlapa-de-comonfort.name: Tlapa de Comonfort
tlapa-de-comonfort.summary: A city in the mountain region of Guerrero, Mexico, whose Nahuatl name means 'place of washing'.

huamuxtitl-n.name: Huamuxtitlán
huamuxtitl-n.summary: A city and seat of its municipality in the southern Mexican state of Guerrero.

marquelia.name: Marquelia
marquelia.summary: City and municipal seat in the southern Mexican state of Guerrero.

mazat-n-chiapas.name: Mazatán
mazat-n-chiapas.summary: A municipality in the Mexican state of Chiapas with an archaeological history dating back to 2500 BC.

san-lorenzo-tenochtitl-n.name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
san-lorenzo-tenochtitl-n.summary: Major Olmec city on Mexico's Gulf Coast, the leading Olmec center from about 1400 to 900 BCE and known for its colossal carved stone heads.

paso-de-la-amada.name: Paso de la Amada
paso-de-la-amada.summary: An archaeological site in Chiapas, Mexico, occupied from about 1800 to 1000 BCE, home to the oldest known Mesoamerican ballcourt and early evidence of social stratification.

mesoamerican-ballgame.name: Mesoamerican ballgame
mesoamerican-ballgame.summary: A ritual sport played across pre-Columbian Mesoamerica from at least 1650 BCE, using a solid rubber ball that players struck mostly with their hips; some ceremonies combined it with human sacrifice.

nakbe.name: Nakbe
nakbe.summary: One of the largest early Maya sites, in Guatemala's Mirador Basin, inhabited from around 1400 BCE until its collapse around 100 to 200 CE.

olmec-colossal-heads.name: Olmec colossal heads
olmec-colossal-heads.summary: Massive carved basalt boulder heads, some over 11 feet tall, made by the Olmec civilization and thought to portray powerful rulers wearing distinctive headdresses.

sierra-de-los-tuxtlas.name: Sierra de Los Tuxtlas
sierra-de-los-tuxtlas.summary: A volcanic mountain range on Mexico's Gulf coast whose basalt, quarried by the Olmec from around 1500–400 BCE, was rafted to their heartland to carve monuments including colossal heads.

guerrero.name: Guerrero
guerrero.summary: A mountainous Mexican state on the Pacific coast, home to Acapulco, named after independence leader and later president Vicente Guerrero.

mixe-zoque-languages.name: Mixe–Zoque
mixe-zoque-languages.summary: A family of languages spoken around Mexico's Isthmus of Tehuantepec, including Mixe and Zoque, with roughly a dozen distinct languages recognized today.

mesoamerican-calendars.name: Mesoamerican calendars
mesoamerican-calendars.summary: A system of calendars used by pre-Columbian Mesoamerican cultures, centered on a 260-day year, for religious observances and divination since about 1100 BCE; still used in parts of Guatemala and Mexico.

izapa.name: Izapa
izapa.summary: A large pre-Columbian archaeological site in Chiapas, Mexico, best known for its occupation during the Late Formative period.

gnomon.name: Gnomon
gnomon.summary: The stationary part of a sundial that casts a shadow, used to measure direction, position or time.

monte-alto-culture.name: Monte Alto culture
monte-alto-culture.summary: A Preclassic culture on Guatemala's Pacific coast, known from the archaeological site of the same name.

potbelly-sculpture.name: Barrigones
potbelly-sculpture.summary: In-the-round sculptures of obese human figures carved from boulders, a non-Maya tradition found in the southern Maya area, likely used in public veneration and rituals led by the ruling elite.

la-democracia-escuintla.name: La Democracia, Escuintla
la-democracia-escuintla.summary: A town and municipality in Guatemala's Escuintla department, notable for the Olmec-influenced carved stone heads of the Monte Alto culture displayed in its town square.

oc-s.name: Ocós
oc-s.summary: A coastal municipality in Guatemala's San Marcos Department, near the Mexican border, which lost about two-thirds of its territory in 2014.

ujuxte.name: Ujuxte
ujuxte.summary: The largest Preclassic Maya site discovered on Guatemala's Pacific coast, located in the Retalhuleu Department.

tlatilco-culture.name: Tlatilco culture
tlatilco-culture.summary: A culture that flourished in Mexico's Valley of Mexico between about 1250 and 800 BCE, marked by growing social complexity, specialized occupations, and long-distance trade linked to Olmec influence.

valley-of-mexico.name: Valley of Mexico
valley-of-mexico.summary: A large basin in the highlands of central Mexico that was home to pre-Columbian civilizations including Teotihuacan and the Aztec Empire, and now contains Mexico City.

lake-texcoco.name: Lake Texcoco
lake-texcoco.summary: A former saline lake in the Valley of Mexico whose island city, Tenochtitlan, became the Aztec capital; it was mostly drained after the Spanish conquest.

pet-n-basin.name: Petén
pet-n-basin.summary: A subregion of the Maya Lowlands in northern Guatemala where major Maya centers such as Tikal and Calakmul flourished.

otomi.name: Otomi
otomi.summary: An Indigenous people of central Mexico numbering over 667,000 in 2015, with a language showing wide regional diversity and many different names for themselves.
